claim: The sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P)/sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor-1 (S1PR1) axis is critically important for lymphocyte egress from lymphoid organs.
source: While the sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P)/sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor-1 (S1PR1) axis is critically important for lymphocyte egress from lymphoid organs, S1PR1-activation also occurs in vascular endothelial cells (ECs), including those of the high-endothelial venules (HEVs) that mediate lymphocyte immigration into lymph nodes (LNs).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract without specific citation, drawing from established scientific consensus.

claim: S1PR1-activation occurs in vascular endothelial cells (ECs), including those of the high-endothelial venules (HEVs) that mediate lymphocyte immigration into lymph nodes (LNs).
source: While the sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P)/sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor-1 (S1PR1) axis is critically important for lymphocyte egress from lymphoid organs, S1PR1-activation also occurs in vascular endothelial cells (ECs), including those of the high-endothelial venules (HEVs) that mediate lymphocyte immigration into lymph nodes (LNs).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: HEVs express LYVE1 during development.
source: To understand the functional significance of the S1P/S1PR1-Gi axis in HEVs, we generated Lyve1;Spns2Δ/Δ conditional knockout mice for the S1P-transporter Spinster-homologue-2 (SPNS2), as HEVs express LYVE1 during development.
evidence: This is stated as a rationale for the experimental approach and is supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: In Lyve1;Spns2Δ/Δ mice HEVs appeared apoptotic.
source: In these mice HEVs appeared apoptotic and were severely impaired in function, morphology and size; leading to markedly hypotrophic peripheral LNs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data including TUNEL assays shown in Figure 3D.

claim: HEVs in Lyve1;Spns2Δ/Δ mice were severely impaired in function, morphology and size.
source: In these mice HEVs appeared apoptotic and were severely impaired in function, morphology and size; leading to markedly hypotrophic peripheral LNs.
evidence: This is supported by multiple experimental observations including microscopy, flow cytometry, and functional assays presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Lyve1;Spns2Δ/Δ mice have markedly hypotrophic peripheral LNs.
source: In these mice HEVs appeared apoptotic and were severely impaired in function, morphology and size; leading to markedly hypotrophic peripheral LNs.
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 1A and quantified in subsequent figures.

claim: Dendritic cells (DCs) were unable to interact with HEVs in Lyve1;Spns2Δ/Δ mice.
source: Dendritic cells (DCs) were unable to interact with HEVs, which was also observed in Cdh5CRE-ERT2;S1pr1Δ/Δ mice and wildtype mice treated with S1PR1-antagonists.
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy and quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3 and Figure 6.

claim: Dendritic cells (DCs) were unable to interact with HEVs in Cdh5CRE-ERT2;S1pr1Δ/Δ mice.
source: Dendritic cells (DCs) were unable to interact with HEVs, which was also observed in Cdh5CRE-ERT2;S1pr1Δ/Δ mice and wildtype mice treated with S1PR1-antagonists.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D-F.

claim: Dendritic cells (DCs) were unable to interact with HEVs in wildtype mice treated with S1PR1-antagonists.
source: Dendritic cells (DCs) were unable to interact with HEVs, which was also observed in Cdh5CRE-ERT2;S1pr1Δ/Δ mice and wildtype mice treated with S1PR1-antagonists.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Wildtype HEVs treated with S1PR1-antagonists in vitro show severely reduced release of the DC-chemoattractant CCL21.
source: Wildtype HEVs treated with S1PR1-antagonists in vitro and Lyve1-deficient HEVs show severely reduced release of the DC-chemoattractant CCL21 in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Lyve1-deficient HEVs show severely reduced release of the DC-chemoattractant CCL21 in vivo.
source: Wildtype HEVs treated with S1PR1-antagonists in vitro and Lyve1-deficient HEVs show severely reduced release of the DC-chemoattractant CCL21 in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry and qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 7A-C.

claim: EC-derived S1P warrants HEV-integrity through autocrine control of S1PR1-Gi signaling.
source: Together, our results reveal that EC-derived S1P warrants HEV-integrity through autocrine control of S1PR1-Gi signaling, and facilitates concomitant HEV-DC interactions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental observations throughout the manuscript.

claim: EC-derived S1P facilitates HEV-DC interactions.
source: Together, our results reveal that EC-derived S1P warrants HEV-integrity through autocrine control of S1PR1-Gi signaling, and facilitates concomitant HEV-DC interactions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental observations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Lymph nodes (LNs) are essential sites for maturation, activation, homeostatic expansion, and tolerance induction of lymphocytes.
source: Lymph nodes (LNs) are essential sites for maturation, activation, homeostatic expansion, and tolerance induction of lymphocytes (Girard et al., 2012; von Andrian and Mempel, 2003), and serve as an immunological interface between the blood and lymph circulatory systems.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature (Girard et al., 2012; von Andrian and Mempel, 2003).

claim: Lymph nodes serve as an immunological interface between the blood and lymph circulatory systems.
source: Lymph nodes (LNs) are essential sites for maturation, activation, homeostatic expansion, and tolerance induction of lymphocytes (Girard et al., 2012; von Andrian and Mempel, 2003), and serve as an immunological interface between the blood and lymph circulatory systems.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Naïve lymphocytes immigrate from the blood through specialized postcapillary venules known as high-endothelial venules (HEVs).
source: In LNs antigens are recognized by recirculating naïve lymphocytes that immigrate from the blood through specialized postcapillary venules known as high-endothelial venules (HEVs) (Girard et al., 2012; Miyasaka and Tanaka, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature (Girard et al., 2012; Miyasaka and Tanaka, 2004).

claim: The entry of naïve T-cells and dendritic cell (DC) precursors from blood into LNs is critically dependent on the interaction of chemokines CCL21 and CCL19 and their receptor CCR7.
source: The entry of naïve T-cells and dendritic cell (DC) precursors from blood, or of effector or memory T-cells and activated DCs from afferent lymphatics into LNs, has been shown to be critically dependent on the interaction of chemokines CCL21 and CCL19 and their receptor CCR7, expressed on lymphocytes or DCs (Förster et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature (Förster et al., 2012).

claim: CCL21 is abundantly produced and secreted by high-endothelial cells and accumulates in the perivascular sheath of the HEVs.
source: Importantly, CCL21 is abundantly produced and secreted by high-endothelial cells and accumulates in the perivascular sheath of the HEVs (Yang et al., 2007; Gunn et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature (Yang et al., 2007; Gunn et al., 1998).

claim: CCL21 facilitates adhesion of rolling lymphocytes and initiates transendothelial migration of T-cells and DC precursors into the LNs.
source: Within the HEV lumen, CCL21 facilitates adhesion of rolling lymphocytes and initiates transendothelial migration of T-cells and DC precursors into the LNs (Yang et al., 2007; Stein et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature (Yang et al., 2007; Stein et al., 2000).

claim: The egress of lymphocytes from the LNs into the lymphatic vasculature is controlled by the lipid-mediator sphingosine-1-phosophate (S1P).
source: On the other hand, the egress of lymphocytes from the LNs into the lymphatic vasculature is controlled by the lipid-mediator sphingosine-1-phosophate (S1P).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Blood endothelial cells (BECs) and lymphatic endothelial cells (LECs) are important sources for providing S1P in blood and lymph, respectively.
source: Through genetic approaches, targeting the enzymes responsible for S1P production, sphingosine kinase-1 (SPHK1) and sphingosine kinase-2 (SPHK2), both blood endothelial cells (BECs) and lymphatic endothelial cells (LECs) were identified as important sources for providing S1P in blood and lymph, respectively (Pappu et al., 2007; Pham et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature (Pappu et al., 2007; Pham et al., 2010).

claim: BECs secrete S1P via the transporter Spinster-homolog-2 (SPNS2).
source: We reported recently that BECs secrete S1P via the transporter Spinster-homolog-2 (SPNS2) (Fukuhara et al., 2012), which had been identified by us and others as a specific S1P transporter in zebra fish (Kawahara et al., 2009; Osborne et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature (Fukuhara et al., 2012; Kawahara et al., 2009; Osborne et al., 2008).

claim: The S1P secretion from BECs by SPNS2 contributes to about 50% of the total S1P in the blood plasma.
source: The S1P secretion from BECs by SPNS2 contributes to about 50% of the total S1P in the blood plasma whereas hematopoietic cells, for example platelets and erythrocytes, release S1P in a SPNS2-independent manner (Fukuhara et al., 2012; Hisano et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature (Fukuhara et al., 2012; Hisano et al., 2012).

claim: Hematopoietic cells, for example platelets and erythrocytes, release S1P in a SPNS2-independent manner.
source: The S1P secretion from BECs by SPNS2 contributes to about 50% of the total S1P in the blood plasma whereas hematopoietic cells, for example platelets and erythrocytes, release S1P in a SPNS2-independent manner (Fukuhara et al., 2012; Hisano et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature (Fukuhara et al., 2012; Hisano et al., 2012).

claim: High-endothelial cells show constitutively active S1PR1-Gi signalling.
source: Here we found that Spns2 is expressed in high-endothelial cells that have been described as showing constitutively active S1PR1-Gi signalling (Kono et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature (Kono et al., 2014).

claim: Spns2 is expressed in high-endothelial cells.
source: Here we found that Spns2 is expressed in high-endothelial cells that have been described as showing constitutively active S1PR1-Gi signalling (Kono et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Lyve1-specific deletion of Spns2 did not affect S1P levels in blood.
source: Lyve1-specific deletion of Spns2 did not affect S1P levels in blood, but did reduce the S1P concentration in lymph fluid to only 14.7% of that seen in lymph of Spns2f/f mice (Figure 1 (B)).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 1B with quantitative measurements.

claim: Lyve1-specific deletion of Spns2 reduced the S1P concentration in lymph fluid to only 14.7% of that seen in lymph of Spns2f/f mice.
source: Lyve1-specific deletion of Spns2 did not affect S1P levels in blood, but did reduce the S1P concentration in lymph fluid to only 14.7% of that seen in lymph of Spns2f/f mice (Figure 1 (B)).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 1B with quantitative measurements.

claim: Sphingosine and glycerol-based lysophospholipid levels in both blood and lymph were comparable between Spns2-deficient and control mice.
source: Nevertheless, sphingosine and glycerol-based lysophospholipid levels in both blood and lymph were comparable between Spns2-deficient and control mice (Figure 1 (B) and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1 with quantitative measurements.

claim: Frequencies and total cell numbers of CD4+ and CD8+ SP T-cells in the thymus of Lyve1;Spns2Δ/Δ mice were comparable to those of Spns2f/f mice.
source: Nonetheless, frequencies and total cell numbers of CD4+ and CD8+ SP T-cells in the thymus of Lyve1;Spns2Δ/Δ mice were comparable to those of Spns2f/f mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 2 (A)), whereas the hypotrophic pLNs of Lyve1;Spns2Δ/Δ mice showed a strong reduction in the total number of cells to only 20.1% of CD4+ and 21.7% of CD8+ SP T-cells, and 59% of mature recirculating (rec.) B-cells (CD19+/CD23+/IgD+; Figure 1 (C–D)).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A with flow cytometry data.

claim: The hypotrophic pLNs of Lyve1;Spns2Δ/Δ mice showed a strong reduction in the total number of cells to only 20.1% of CD4+ and 21.7% of CD8+ SP T-cells.
source: Nonetheless, frequencies and total cell numbers of CD4+ and CD8+ SP T-cells in the thymus of Lyve1;Spns2Δ/Δ mice were comparable to those of Spns2f/f mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 2 (A)), whereas the hypotrophic pLNs of Lyve1;Spns2Δ/Δ mice showed a strong reduction in the total number of cells to only 20.1% of CD4+ and 21.7% of CD8+ SP T-cells, and 59% of mature recirculating (rec.) B-cells (CD19+/CD23+/IgD+; Figure 1 (C–D)).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 1C-D with flow cytometry data.

claim: The hypotrophic pLNs of Lyve1;Spns2Δ/Δ mice showed 59% of mature recirculating (rec.) B-cells compared to controls.
source: Nonetheless, frequencies and total cell numbers of CD4+ and CD8+ SP T-cells in the thymus of Lyve1;Spns2Δ/Δ mice were comparable to those of Spns2f/f mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 2 (A)), whereas the hypotrophic pLNs of Lyve1;Spns2Δ/Δ mice showed a strong reduction in the total number of cells to only 20.1% of CD4+ and 21.7% of CD8+ SP T-cells, and 59% of mature recirculating (rec.) B-cells (CD19+/CD23+/IgD+; Figure 1 (C–D)).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 1C-D with flow cytometry data.

claim: In the spleen of Lyve1;Spns2Δ/Δ mice, follicular (FO) B-cells were reduced to 43.5%.
source: In the spleen of Lyve1;Spns2Δ/Δ mice, follicular (FO) B-cells were reduced to 43.5%, whereas marginal zone (MZ) B-cells were increased to 55% (Figure 1—figure supplement 2 (D-E)).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D-E with flow cytometry data.

claim: In the spleen of Lyve1;Spns2Δ/Δ mice, marginal zone (MZ) B-cells were increased to 55%.
source: In the spleen of Lyve1;Spns2Δ/Δ mice, follicular (FO) B-cells were reduced to 43.5%, whereas marginal zone (MZ) B-cells were increased to 55% (Figure 1—figure supplement 2 (D-E)).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D-E with flow cytometry data.

claim: Flow cytometric analyses of the lymph collected from the cisterna chyli of Lyve1;Spns2Δ/Δ mice confirmed a complete absence of recirculating lymphocytes.
source: Consistent with the strong reduction of lymph S1P-levels (Figure 1 (B)), flow cytometric analyses of the lymph collected from the cisterna chyli of Lyve1;Spns2Δ/Δ mice confirmed a complete absence of recirculating lymphocytes (Figure 2 (A)), indicating severe impairment of lymphocyte-egress into the lymphatics from pLNs.
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 2A with flow cytometry data.

claim: Immigration into pLNs of Lyve1;Spns2Δ/Δ mice was ~5.2 fold less efficient than into pLNs of Spns2f/f mice.
source: Flow cytometric analyses recorded two hours after injection of cells showed that immigration into pLNs of Lyve1;Spns2Δ/Δ mice was ~5.2 fold less efficient than into pLNs of Spns2f/f mice (Figure 2 (C)).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 2C with flow cytometry data from adoptive transfer experiments.

claim: Development of PNAd+ HEVs appear to be severely compromised in pLNs of Lyve1;Spns2Δ/Δ mice.
source: Given that cellular immigration into pLNs was strongly reduced, we next sought to determine if Lyve1 specific ablation of Spns2 had an effect on HEVs and found that development of PNAd+ HEVs appear to be severely compromised in pLNs of Lyve1;Spns2Δ/Δ mice (Figure 2 (D)).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 2D with immunohistochemistry.

claim: The frequencies of CD45-/CD31+/PNAd+ high-endothelial cells isolated from pLNs of Lyve1;Spns2Δ/Δ were ~2.3 fold reduced compared to controls.
source: In agreement with this observation in IHC, the frequencies of CD45-/CD31+/PNAd+ high-endothelial cells isolated from pLNs of Lyve1;Spns2Δ/Δ were ~2.3 fold reduced and total cell numbers were ~10.3 fold decreased in comparison to the controls when analysed by FACS (Figure 2 (E)).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 2E with flow cytometry data.

claim: Total cell numbers of CD45-/CD31+/PNAd+ high-endothelial cells isolated from pLNs of Lyve1;Spns2Δ/Δ were ~10.3 fold decreased compared to controls.
source: In agreement with this observation in IHC, the frequencies of CD45-/CD31+/PNAd+ high-endothelial cells isolated from pLNs of Lyve1;Spns2Δ/Δ were ~2.3 fold reduced and total cell numbers were ~10.3 fold decreased in comparison to the controls when analysed by FACS (Figure 2 (E)).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 2E with flow cytometry data.

claim: More than 90% of HEVs of pLNs simultaneously expressed PNAd and tdTOMATO in Lyve1;tdTomato mice.
source: We revealed that more than 90% of HEVs of pLNs simultaneously expressed PNAd and tdTOMATO in Lyve1;tdTomato mice, but did not express LYVE1 at detectable levels on the cell surface (Figure 2—figure supplement 1 (A-B)).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-B with confocal microscopy and flow cytometry data.

claim: HEVs in Lyve1;tdTomato mice did not express LYVE1 at detectable levels on the cell surface.
source: We revealed that more than 90% of HEVs of pLNs simultaneously expressed PNAd and tdTOMATO in Lyve1;tdTomato mice, but did not express LYVE1 at detectable levels on the cell surface (Figure 2—figure supplement 1 (A-B)).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-B with confocal microscopy and flow cytometry data.

claim: Quantitative RT-PCR analyses confirmed the deletion of Spns2 in purified CD45-/CD31+/PNAd+ high-endothelial cells and CD45-/LYVE1+ LECs in pLNs of Lyve1;Spns2Δ/Δ mice.
source: However, quantitative RT-PCR analyses confirmed the deletion of Spns2 in purified CD45-/CD31+/PNAd+ high-endothelial cells and CD45-/LYVE1+ LECs in pLNs of Lyve1;Spns2Δ/Δ mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1 (D)).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D with qRT-PCR data.

claim: iLNs of E16.5 expressed LYVE1 weakly on MAdCAM-1+/PNAd-endothelial cells that are evocative in localization and morphology to high-endothelial cell progenitors.
source: iLNs of E16.5 expressed LYVE1 weakly on MAdCAM-1+/PNAd-endothelial cells that are evocative in localization and morphology to high-endothelial cell progenitors (Figure 2—figure supplement 1 (E), top).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E with confocal microscopy of embryonic tissue.

claim: Triple-positive MAdCAM-1+/PNAd+/LYVE1+ HEVs were found in iLNs of E18.5.
source: Furthermore, triple-positive MAdCAM-1+/PNAd+/LYVE1+ HEVs were found in iLNs of E18.5 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1 (E), bottom).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E with confocal microscopy of embryonic tissue.

claim: DCs play a critical role in the maintenance of HEV architecture and function in pLNs.
source: Given that DCs play a critical role in the maintenance of HEV architecture and function in pLNs (Moussion and Girard, 2011; Wendland et al., 2011), we analysed DC homeostasis in Lyve1;Spns2Δ/Δ mice.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature (Moussion and Girard, 2011; Wendland et al., 2011).

claim: Total numbers of resident DCs (rDCs) and mDCs in pLNs of Lyve1;Spns2Δ/Δ mice were reduced to 65.2% (rDCs) and 58.4% (mDCs) compared to Spns2f/f mice.
source: However, in comparison to Spns2f/f mice total numbers of resident DCs (rDCs) and mDCs in pLNs of Lyve1;Spns2Δ/Δ mice were reduced to 65.2% (rDCs) and 58.4% (mDCs) indicating reduced immigration of DCs (Figure 3 (A)).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 3A with flow cytometry data.

claim: Endogenous DCs were in close proximity to PNAd+ HEVs in pLNs of Spns2f/f mice.
source: We observed that endogenous DCs were in close proximity to PNAd+ HEVs in pLNs of Spns2f/f mice (Figure 3 (B), Figure 3—figure supplement 1 (B)).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B with confocal microscopy.

claim: Endogenous DCs were absent in areas adjacent to PNAd+ HEVs in pLNs of Lyve1;Spns2Δ/Δ mice.
source: In contrast, endogenous DCs were absent in areas adjacent to PNAd+ HEVs in pLNs of Lyve1;Spns2Δ/Δ mice (Figure 3 (B)), thus unlikely to provide angiogenic factors to high-endothelial cells.
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 3B with confocal microscopy.

claim: High-endothelial cells lost their characteristic cuboidal morphology in pLNs of Lyve1;Spns2Δ/Δ mice.
source: Moreover, high-endothelial cells lost their characteristic cuboidal morphology and nuclei of high-endothelial cells appear deformed in comparison to HEVs in pLNs of Spns2f/f mice (Figure 3 (C)).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 3C with transmission electron microscopy.

claim: A flow cytometric TUNEL assay showed a dramatic ~25 fold increase of apoptotic CD45-/CD31+/PNAd+ high-endothelial cells in pLNs isolated from Lyve1;Spns2Δ/Δ mice in comparison to the controls.
source: Indeed, a flow cytometric terminal deoxynucleotidyl ransferase (TdT) dUTP Nick-End Labeling (TUNEL) assay showed a dramatic ~25 fold increase of apoptotic CD45-/CD31+/PNAd+ high-endothelial cells in pLNs isolated from Lyve1;Spns2Δ/Δ mice in comparison to the controls (Figure 3 (D)).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 3D with flow cytometry TUNEL assay data.

claim: BMDCs immigrated through afferent lymphatics into pLNs of Lyve1;Spns2Δ/Δ mice in frequencies comparable to those of the controls.
source: BMDCs immigrated through afferent lymphatics into pLNs of Lyve1;Spns2Δ/Δ mice in frequencies comparable to those of the controls.
evidence: This is stated based on experimental observations from BMDC transfer experiments.

claim: Total numbers of homed BMDCs were strongly reduced particularly in a restricted area 40 μm from the basal lamina of HEVs in pLNs of Lyve1;Spns2Δ/Δ mice when compared to BMDCs in pLNs of Spns2f/f mice.
source: Strikingly, total numbers of homed BMDCs were strongly reduced particularly in a restricted area 40 μm from the basal lamina of HEVs in pLNs of Lyve1;Spns2Δ/Δ mice when compared to BMDCs in pLNs of Spns2f/f mice (Figure 3 (F–H)).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 3F-H with confocal microscopy and quantitative analysis.

claim: Treatment with agonistic anti-LTβr antibody and recombinant LTα1/β2 protein partially rescued total high-endothelial cell numbers and HEV morphology in pLNs of Lyve1;Spns2Δ/Δ mice.
source: This hypothesis was supported by the partial rescue of total high-endothelial cell numbers and HEV morphology in pLNs of Lyve1;Spns2Δ/Δ mice observed upon 10 weeks of treatment with agonistic anti-LTβr antibody and recombinant LTα1/β2 protein (Figure 4 (A–D)).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 4A-D with confocal microscopy and quantitative analysis.

claim: Treatment with agonistic anti-LTβr antibody and recombinant LTα1/β2 protein was unable to rescue the size of pLNs in Lyve1;Spns2Δ/Δ mice.
source: While this treatment was unable to rescue the size of pLNs (Figure 4 (A–C)), it significantly increased the total numbers of HEVs and the average PNAd+ area per LN-section (Figure 4 (B–D)).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 4A-C with confocal microscopy and quantitative analysis.

claim: Treatment with agonistic anti-LTβr antibody and recombinant LTα1/β2 protein significantly increased the total numbers of HEVs and the average PNAd+ area per LN-section in Lyve1;Spns2Δ/Δ mice.
source: While this treatment was unable to rescue the size of pLNs (Figure 4 (A–C)), it significantly increased the total numbers of HEVs and the average PNAd+ area per LN-section (Figure 4 (B–D)).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 4B-D with confocal microscopy and quantitative analysis.

claim: FTY720 targets four of the five S1PRs (S1PR1 and S1PR3-5).
source: FTY720 targets four of the five S1PRs (S1PR1 and S1PR3-5) (Brinkmann et al., 2002) and should therefore induce impaired HEV-DC interactions of lymph-derived BMDCs in pLNs of recipient mice.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature (Brinkmann et al., 2002).

claim: 24 hr after footpad injection of BMDCs into FTY720-treated mice, there was a severe reduction of homed BMDCs in a restricted area around HEVs within an extended area 70 μm from the basal lamina of HEVs.
source: Again, 24 hr after footpad injection we observed a severe reduction of homed BMDCs in a restricted area around HEVs within an extended area 70 μm from the basal lamina of HEVs (Figure 5 (B–D)), in agreement with the hypothesis that HEV-derived S1P controls DC localization in pLNs.
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 5B-D with confocal microscopy and quantitative analysis.

claim: HEVs express S1PR1 and activate strong S1PR1-Gi signalling.
source: Indeed, HEVs have been described to express S1PR1 and activate strong S1PR1-Gi signalling (Kono et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature (Kono et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2014).

claim: Abrogation of S1PR1-Gi signalling with W146 induced impaired HEV-DC interactions in a restricted area within 40 μm from the basal lamina of HEVs in pLNs of recipient mice.
source: Interestingly, abrogation of S1PR1-Gi signalling with W146 also induced impaired HEV-DC interactions in a restricted area within 40 μm from the basal lamina of HEVs in pLNs of recipient mice (Figure 5 (F) and Figure 5—figure supplement 1 (A-B)).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-B with confocal microscopy and quantitative analysis.

claim: Application of TY52156, and the concomitant block of S1PR3-signalling, did not affect localization of DCs around HEVs.
source: However, application of TY52156, and the concomitant block of S1PR3-signalling, did not affect localization of DCs around HEVs (Figure 5 (G) and Figure 5—figure supplement 1 (C-D)).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 5G and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C-D with confocal microscopy and quantitative analysis.

claim: HEV-DC interactions are dependent on S1PR1- but not S1PR3 signalling either in DCs or in high-endothelial cells.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that HEV-DC interactions are dependent on S1PR1- but not S1PR3 signalling either in DCs or in high-endothelial cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations with S1PR1 and S1PR3 antagonists.

claim: S1PR1 is expressed on PNAd+ HEVs in pLNs of Spns2f/f and Lyve1;Spns2Δ/Δ mice.
source: Immunohistochemistry and FACS revealed S1PR1 expression on PNAd+ HEVs in pLNs of Spns2f/f and Lyve1;Spns2Δ/Δ mice (Figure 6 (A–B)).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 6A-B with immunohistochemistry and flow cytometry.

claim: PNAd+ HEVs in pLNs of Spns2f/f showed distinct phosphorylation of Akt in contrast to the reduced levels of pAkt in high-endothelial cells in pLNs of Lyve1;Spns2Δ/Δ mice.
source: PNAd+ HEVs in pLNs of Spns2f/f showed distinct phosphorylation of Akt in contrast to the reduced levels of pAkt in high-endothelial cells in pLNs of Lyve1;Spns2Δ/Δ mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 1 (E)).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E with immunofluorescence microscopy.

claim: Cdh5CRE-ERT2;S1pr1Δ/Δ mice did not show any differences in CD4 or CD8 single-positive T-cell and mature rec. B-cell numbers in peripheral blood or pLNs.
source: Cdh5CRE-ERT2;S1pr1Δ/Δ mice did not show any differences in CD4 or CD8 single-positive T-cell and mature rec. B-cell numbers in peripheral blood or pLNs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1 (C-D)).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C-D with flow cytometry data.

claim: When wildtype BMDCs were injected into the footpad of Cdh5CRE-ERT2;S1pr1Δ/Δ mice, there was a remarkable impairment of total DC-numbers within a restricted area of 0–60 μm around the basal lamina of HEVs.
source: Strikingly, in these mice, mature wildtype BMDCs fail to co-localize with S1pr1-deficient HEVs, as also observed in Lyve1;Spns2Δ/Δ mice or WT mice treated with S1PR1-antagonists. Indeed, when we performed WT BMDC injections into the footpad of Cdh5CRE-ERT2;S1pr1Δ/Δ mice (Figure 6 (C)) and analysed HEV-DC interactions 24 hr later, we could detect a remarkable impairment of total DC-numbers within a restricted area of 0–60 μm around the basal lamina of HEVs (Figure 6 (D–F)), while no differences in DC-positioning close to cortical lymphatics were observed (Figure 6—figure supplement 1 (E-G)).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 6D-F with confocal microscopy and quantitative analysis.

claim: No differences in DC-positioning close to cortical lymphatics were observed in Cdh5CRE-ERT2;S1pr1Δ/Δ mice.

claim: CCR7 and its ligand CCL21 are essentially involved in the extravasation of T- and B-cells through lymph node HEVs.

evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature (MartIn-Fontecha et al., 2003; Ohl et al., 2004).

evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature (MartIn-Fontecha et al., 2003; Ohl et al., 2004).

evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature (Yang et al., 2007; Gunn et al., 1998).

claim: Depletion of DCs in vivo led to the downregulation of PNAd and HEV-specific genes.
source: Depletion of DCs in vivo led to the downregulation of PNAd and HEV-specific genes (Moussion and Girard, 2011) that is Glycam-1, FucT-VII and Chst4, the latter two encoding for the HEV-unique enzymes fucosyltransferase-7 and N-acetylglucosamine 6-O-sulphotransferase 2 (GlcNAc6ST-2), respectively (Rosen, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature (Moussion and Girard, 2011; Rosen, 2004).

claim: BECs secrete S1P via the transporter Spinster-homolog-2 (SPNS2).

evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature (Fukuhara et al., 2012; Kawahara et al., 2009; Osborne et al., 2008).

claim: ECs account for the formation of an S1P gradient responsible for lymphocyte egress from thymus and secondary lymphoid organs.
source: Therefore, influenced by the activities and distribution of degradative and biosynthetic enzymes, ECs account for the formation of an S1P gradient responsible for lymphocyte egress from thymus and secondary lymphoid organs (Fukuhara et al., 2012; Hisano et al., 2012; Mendoza et al., 2012; Nagahashi et al., 2013; Nijnik et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature (Fukuhara et al., 2012; Hisano et al., 2012; Mendoza et al., 2012; Nagahashi et al., 2013; Nijnik et al., 2012).

claim: LYVE1+ LECs make a significant contribution to lymph S1P-levels by secreting S1P via SPNS2 into the lymphatics.
source: These results are compatible with the hypothesis that LYVE1+ LECs make a significant contribution to lymph S1P-levels by secreting S1P via SPNS2 into the lymphatics and thereby control lymphocyte egress from secondary lymphoid organs into the lymphatic system.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations showing reduced S1P in lymph but not blood of Lyve1;Spns2Δ/Δ mice.

claim: LYVE1+ LECs control lymphocyte egress from secondary lymphoid organs into the lymphatic system.
source: These results are compatible with the hypothesis that LYVE1+ LECs make a significant contribution to lymph S1P-levels by secreting S1P via SPNS2 into the lymphatics and thereby control lymphocyte egress from secondary lymphoid organs into the lymphatic system.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations showing impaired lymphocyte egress in Lyve1;Spns2Δ/Δ mice.
